title: Water rocket 1: pressure and mass
summary: Launch a 2 litre bottle water rocket, time each flight to estimate its height, and see how the amount of water changes what the launch does.
materials: water rocket launcher (or a bottle launcher) and a bike pump

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
A new build opens: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: what makes a water rocket fly, and does more water make it fly higher?

Imagine: a bottle holding both pressurised air and water, launched nozzle down. The air pushes the water out fast, and the escaping water pushes the bottle the other way.

Plan: on graph paper, list three water volumes to test, for example a third, a half and two thirds of the bottle. Use the same number of pump strokes for every launch, and decide how you will time each flight with the stopwatch.

figure.alt: A bottle rocket shown nozzle-down: pressurized air sits in the top of the bottle above a dashed line, water fills the bottom, and the nozzle points downward at the base. An arrow shows water shooting out fast through the nozzle; an opposite arrow above the bottle shows the thrust that pushes the rocket upward in reaction.

items.s: Escaping water pushes the rocket back

steps.title: Pressure becomes thrust
steps.body:
Pumping air into a sealed bottle raises the pressure inside far above the air outside. When the nozzle releases, that pressure pushes the water out through the small opening, fast. Pushing the water one way pushes the bottle the other way, the same idea that fires the water out of a garden hose when you squeeze it.

Water matters because it is heavy compared with air. A rocket with more water has more mass to push out the back. That gives a stronger push while it lasts, but also more total mass to lift off the pad. Many water rockets fly highest with roughly a third of the bottle filled with water, though the best amount depends on the launcher and the pressure used.

Once the flight is in the air, timing it gives a height estimate. For a mostly vertical flight, the rocket spends about half its total flight time going up. Height is then roughly half of 9.8 metres per second squared, times half the total flight time, squared.

figure.alt: A launch setup: the rocket sits on the launcher at left. A dashed safe-distance line separates the launch pad from where everyone stands back wearing safety glasses. Dots mark the adult who operates the release near the launcher, and the observer holding the stopwatch that times each flight, both behind the safe-distance line.

items.s: Launch setup: safe distance and the adult's release

steps.title: Launch three water volumes
steps.body:
With an adult, set up the launcher on a clear, open patch of ground, well away from people, windows and power lines. Everyone at the launch, including the adult, wears safety glasses.

Measure the water into the bottle with the jug, then seal it on the launcher. Pump the same number of strokes for every single launch, since the water volume is the only thing being tested today.

An adult always operates the release. Everyone stands back at a safe distance before any pumping starts, and nobody approaches the rocket until it has landed and the launcher is clearly empty.

Time each flight from the moment it leaves the launcher to the moment it lands, with the stopwatch. Launch three water volumes, three times each, nine flights in total, and use each volume's median flight time.
checklist: An adult supervised every launch and operated the release each time
Everyone wore safety glasses and stood at a safe distance before pumping began
The same number of pump strokes was used for every launch
Three water volumes were each launched three times and timed with the stopwatch

steps.title: Water volume versus flight time
steps.body:
The bottle, the launcher and the number of pump strokes stay the same for every row. Only the amount of water changes.

Launch three water volumes, three times each, nine rows in total. For each flight, write the water volume in millilitres and the total flight time in seconds.
steps.question: Which water volume gave the longest flight time, and about how many seconds longer was it than the shortest?

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. Classics this week: a seal that leaks air before launch, which drops the pressure and gives a weak, short flight that does not belong in the data.

Also watch for a stopwatch started a beat late, and pump strokes that quietly drift between launches because nobody counted them out loud.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the rocket on the launcher before a launch, with safety glasses visible, next to your graph paper sketch with all nine flight times written on it

extras.title: Now hold the water and change the pressure
extras.body:
Predict first: will more pump strokes at the same water volume make the rocket fly higher? Write your answer in the Maker's Log, with a guess for how many seconds the flight time will grow.

Measure it with the week's own kit. Pick the water volume that flew longest in the main test and use it for every launch here. Launch it with a low number of pump strokes, counted out loud, and time the flight. Launch it again with a much higher number of pump strokes, same water volume, and time it. Repeat each pump count three times and write the median flight time for each.

Compare: line up the two pump counts' median flight times next to your prediction.

Teach it: explain to the family which change mattered more for how high the rocket went, swapping the water volume from the main test or swapping the pressure here.
